title: Train a 310T or Hire One: What the 2026 Numbers Say
excerpt: Ontario certified 436 Truck and Coach technicians in all of 2025. Ottawa rewrote the apprenticeship funding stack in April, two grants died the year before that, and only 19.9% of apprentices ever certify. What that means if you are deciding between training someone and hiring someone.
author: Certus Technical Search
content:
Ontario issued 436 Certificates of Qualification in Truck and Coach Technician in all of 2025. That is the whole province, finished and certified, for the year.

Sooner or later every shop owner does the arithmetic on that and asks whether it would be easier to grow their own. In 2026 the answer moved, because Ottawa rewrote the funding stack in April and two grants that may still be sitting in your bookkeeper's spreadsheet ended the year before that.

*Current as of September 2026. The federal programs below are moving; confirm before you file.*

## What you can claim right now

**Federal Apprenticeship Job Creation Tax Credit.** 10% of eligible wages to a maximum of $2,000 per apprentice per year, covering the first 24 months of a Red Seal program. You claim it on your return.

**Ontario Achievement Incentive.** Up to $17,000 per apprentice, paid to the sponsor. Up to $2,000 at registration for youth and under-represented apprentices, $1,000 for each completed in-class level with enhancements available on top, and $1,000 at certification.

**Ontario Tools Grant.** $1,000 for motive power trades. Motive power draws the highest tier here, against $600 for construction and industrial and $400 for service.

**Ontario Apprenticeship Completion Employer Bonus.** $1,000, taxable, paid on certification.

**Canada Apprentice Loan.** $4,000 interest-free per technical training period to a $20,000 lifetime maximum, available everywhere except Quebec. The money goes to the apprentice rather than to you, but it takes away one of the reasons people walk during in-school.

## What ended, and what has not started

The Apprenticeship Incentive Grant and the Apprenticeship Completion Grant both closed on 31 March 2025. If either one is still in a spreadsheet somewhere in your office, take it out.

In April 2026 the federal government announced Team Canada Strong: $6 billion over five years aimed at 80,000 to 100,000 new Red Seal trades workers, with a stated goal of cutting time to certification in half. Inside it are a $2 billion apprenticeship service offering up to $10,000 toward a first-year apprentice's salary, a $5,000 Red Seal completion bonus, and a training grant of $400 a week during mandatory in-class time up to $16,000, paid on top of EI.

Watch the in-class grant. In-school is where apprentices disappear, because for several weeks they stop earning shop wages and the household bills carry on as normal. Paying them through those weeks goes straight at the failure point instead of around it.

The intake window has been announced but has not opened. Budget on the money that exists today and treat Team Canada Strong as upside.

## What the return actually looks like

The Canadian Apprenticeship Forum surveyed 533 British Columbia employers about their 2022 apprentices and worked out the return per dollar invested, by trade:

- Industrial Mechanic (Millwright): $1.50
- Heavy Duty Equipment Technician: $1.41
- Automotive Service Technician: $1.32

There is no Truck and Transport Mechanic line in that study, so HDET and AST are the closest proxies available. Every trade near this work returned more than it cost, and the industrial trades came out ahead of construction.

## The completion rate

Statistics Canada's 2024 figures, released last December, show 101,541 new apprenticeship registrations, up 5.9% and the highest since the series started. Certifications came in at 46,971, up 1.0%, still 9.6% below pre-pandemic levels.

Underneath those totals: 19.9% certification, 30.9% discontinuation, roughly half still in progress.

Put the two sections together and the picture is clear enough. Apprenticeship returns somewhere around $1.40 on the dollar for the people who finish, and close to a third of them do not finish. None of it helps a bay you need covered this quarter. A 310T is 6,720 hours, 6,000 on the job and 720 in school across three levels, which works out to roughly three and a half years. A 421A is 7,000 hours.

One number cuts the other way. Heavy duty equipment mechanic certifications rose 41.5% in 2024 and are now past 2019 levels. That corner of the trade is recovering faster than the general shortage story suggests.

## Who can legally work on Monday morning

In Ontario, 310T is compulsory and 421A is not.

To work in Truck and Coach, a person needs a Registered Training Agreement, a Provisional Certificate of Qualification, or a Certificate of Qualification, and it has to be kept current. Heavy Duty Equipment Technician carries no equivalent requirement.

In practice, an uncertified body can work heavy equipment in Ontario and cannot work trucks and coaches. Shops get this wrong often enough that you should check your own roster before an inspector does it for you.

Truck and transport is also compulsory in Nova Scotia and Alberta and voluntary in the rest of the country. Quebec runs a different model entirely, training heavy-vehicle mechanics through a school-based 1,800-hour DEP rather than employer-sponsored apprenticeship, so most of the above does not apply there.

## How to decide

Build if you have a licensed journeyperson with the patience to teach, enough steady work to carry someone through three levels, and a vacancy you are trying to prevent in 2029 rather than fill in November.

Buy if the bay is empty now. The 19.9% certification rate is the argument against using apprenticeship as a recruiting plan, and 436 certificates a year in Ontario is the argument for looking after the licensed people already on your payroll.

Most shops end up doing some of both. The ones that get into trouble are usually running only one.
